html:
Dhar Tichitt is a line of sandstone cliffs in southern Mauritania, at the edge of the Sahara, where people built hundreds of stone villages between about 2200 and 400 BCE. They are among the earliest complex settlements in West Africa.

The villagers of what archaeologists call the Tichitt culture herded cattle and grew crops, above all pearl millet, which was domesticated in this part of the Sahel. They built dry stone walls around houses and cattle pens, some villages large enough to need a hierarchy of centres and smaller hamlets.

As the Sahara dried further and raiders pressed in, the people moved south toward the Niger. Many scholars think they were ancestors of the Soninke, the people who later founded Ghana, the first great empire of West Africa. The cliffs also hold rock art and sit on old routes later used by the trans-Saharan trade.
